37-014.r: Correct pair: lexicography → compiling dictionaries. Philology → language structure and history; entomology → insects; iconography → idols and arts.

37-015.r: Lexicography → compilation of dictionaries (their design, compiling and evaluation).

37-016.r: Viticulture → science, production and study of grapes (vineyards).

37-017.r: Vermiculture → raising (cultivating) earthworms, which turn organic waste into nutrient-rich soil.

37-019.r: Genetics → study of genes, heredity and variations in living organisms.

37-020.r: Gerontology → scientific study of old age, the ageing process and problems of old people.

37-021.r: Old age and ageing → gerontology. Oncology → cancer; teratology → abnormal development; ornithology → birds.

37-023.r: Pedology → study of soil: its formation, morphology and classification.

37-024.r: Bones → osteology. Orology → mountains; serology → serum; geology → Earth's interior and its matter.

37-026.r: Study of snakes → serpentology. Herpetology → amphibians and reptiles (snakes included); ornithology → birds; ichthyology → fish.
37-026.t: Herpetology covers all reptiles and amphibians; serpentology is snakes only.

37-027.r: Odd one out → psychology (study of mind and behaviour); physiology, pathology and bacteriology are branches of biology.

37-028.r: Hydroponics → growing plants without soil in mineral nutrient solutions (soilless culture); sand, perlite or gravel may support roots.

38-001.r: Epochs, oldest to newest → Paleocene, Eocene, Oligocene, Miocene, Pliocene, Pleistocene, Holocene (present).
38-001.h: Please Eat Old Mangoes, Plums, Pears Happily (P-E-O-M-P-P-H).

38-002.r: Primitive Earth's atmosphere → reducing, with no free oxygen; rich in methane, ammonia, water vapour, CO2, CO, nitrogen, hydrogen.

38-003.r: True: Earth's magnetic field reverses every few hundred thousand years (last about 780 thousand years ago); life modified the early atmosphere. False: early Earth had 54% oxygen → 1, 3.

38-004.r: Life on Earth → emerged about 2,000,000,000 years ago (per the book); Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.

38-005.r: Oldest organism (of options) → blue-green algae (cyanobacteria): photosynthetic; their oxygen changed life on Earth.

38-006.r: 'The Origin of Species' (1859) → Charles Darwin; explains natural selection; foundation of evolutionary biology.

38-007.r: Darwin's natural selection → overproduction, struggle for existence and variation, survival of the fittest → all of the above ('On the Origin of Species', 1859).

38-009.r: First to explain evolution → Lamarck (French): inheritance of acquired characteristics, presented 1801; book 'Philosophie Zoologique', 1809.

38-010.r: Mutation theory of evolution → Hugo de Vries: new species arise from sudden heritable variations (mutations), not continuous variations.

38-011.r: Mutation theory → De Vries; evolution → Darwin; one gene one enzyme → Beadle and Tatum; operon concept → Jacob and Monod.

38-012.r: Main factor of evolution (Darwin) → natural selection.

38-013.r: Loss of limbs in snakes → Lamarck's use and disuse of organs: organs not used are lost, and acquired characters are inherited.

38-014.r: Large-scale diversity → mutation: gene and chromosomal mutations are the ultimate 'raw material' of evolution; recombination adds variability.

38-015.r: Origin of new species → mutation: permanent change in the genome's nucleotide sequence (from radiation, chemical mutagens, replication errors).

38-016.r: Latest ancestor of modern humans → Cro-Magnon man, first early modern humans (remains about 43,000 years old); brain about 1,600 cc.

38-017.r: Denisovans → extinct archaic human species of Asia; identified in 2010 from DNA of a finger bone dug up (2008) in Denisova Cave, Altai Mountains, Siberia.

38-018.r: Archaeopteryx → most ancient (first) bird, Jurassic, about 150 million years ago; connecting link between reptiles (Reptilia) and birds (Aves).

38-020.r: Mammoth → linked to the elephant (options); strictly, mammoths and modern elephants share a common ancestor from about 6 million years ago.

38-021.r: Dinosaurs → Mesozoic reptiles; Mesozoic era ('age of dinosaurs') about 250 to 65 million years ago: Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous.

38-023.r: Correct evolutionary order → salamander (amphibian, about 360 million years ago) → python (reptile, about 300) → kangaroo (marsupial mammal, about 145).

39-001.r: Plant classification, higher to lower → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.
39-001.h: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.

39-003.r: Species → group of individuals with fundamental similarities; related species → genus; genera → family; related families → order.

39-004.r: First to use vascular tissues in plant classification → A.P. de Candolle (Swiss), early 19th century: Vasculares (with vascular bundles) and Cellulares (without).

39-005.r: Largest number of identified species → insects (class Insecta, phylum Arthropoda): over 1 million of about 1.5 million described animal species.

39-006.r: Bacteria discovered by → Antony van Leeuwenhoek, father of microbiology (born 24 October 1632, Delft, Netherlands).

39-007.r: Bacteria (mostly 0.5 to 5.0 micron) → seen with a compound microscope, which magnifies 1500-2000 times.

39-008.r: A true: some bacteria (autotrophs) make food by photosynthesis or chemosynthesis. R false: bacteria have no chloroplasts; phototrophic bacteria use bacteriochlorophylls.

39-009.r: Bacteria → single-celled prokaryotes with no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; not on any listed 'borderline' → none of the above.

39-010.r: Gram-positive vs Gram-negative → differ in cell wall: Gram-positive thick, many peptidoglycan layers; Gram-negative thin wall plus an outer lipid membrane.

39-011.r: Smallest organism capable of autonomous growth and reproduction → mycoplasma.

39-012.r: Amoeba reproduces by binary fission, an asexual method of unicellular organisms → A and R true, R explains A (book). Paramecium can reproduce both asexually and sexually.

39-013.r: The book gives no single answer (*): spore formation (asexual) occurs in fungi, algae and ferns (also bacteria, mosses), so more than one option is right.

39-014.r: Bacteria and fungi → can be cultured on artificial media (nutrient agar, dextrose agar); viruses need living host cells → 1 and 2 only.

39-015.r: Warm-blooded animals (mammals, birds) → keep body temperature constant, making or losing heat as needed (homeostasis).

39-016.r: Not correct: all echinoderms are viviparous → echinoderms (starfish, sea urchins) usually have external fertilization and a free-swimming larva. Roundworm lacks circulatory system; bony fish have swim bladder.

39-017.r: No blood but respires → Hydra; gas exchange and excretion happen by simple diffusion.

39-018.r: Not a fish → starfish (sea star, phylum Echinodermata; no gills, scales or fins); sawfish, pipefish, guitarfish are fishes.

39-019.r: True fish → catfish (ray-finned fish, cat-like barbels). Silverfish → insect; crayfish → crustacean; jellyfish → gelatinous marine animal (Aurelia).
39-019.t: Names ending in 'fish' are not always fish.

39-020.r: True fish → seahorse (genus Hippocampus, a bony fish; 45 species). Starfish → echinoderm; jellyfish → Cnidaria; hagfish → Cyclostomata.

39-022.r: Bones in a shark → 0; sharks, skates and rays are cartilaginous fish with skeletons of cartilage and connective tissue.

39-023.r: Not a bird → Golden Mahseer (Tor putitora), an endangered Himalayan fish; Indian Nightjar, Spoonbill and White Ibis are birds.

39-024.r: Largest mammal → whale; the blue whale is the largest animal ever (33 m, over 180 tons); pygmy sperm whale only 3.5 m.

39-027.r: Largest toothed whale → sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus): males up to 20 m, 35 to 45 tons.

39-028.r: Egg-laying mammal → echidna (spiny anteater, a monotreme); echidnas and the platypus are the only living egg-laying mammals (Australia, New Guinea).

39-030.r: Flying mammal → bat (order Chiroptera): webbed forelimb wings, the only mammal with true sustained flight; not a bird (Aves).

39-032.r: The book gives no single answer (*): both statements wrong now; the 2022 amendment moved the flying fox from Schedule V (vermin) to Schedule II; it eats fruit/nectar, not blood.
